title: The "Team Mom" Job Is Unpaid Labor. We Need to Stop Pretending It Isn't.
description: Every gym has one parent doing a dozen unpaid hours a week of work the gym used to pay an admin to do. It's time we called that what it is.
ogDescription: The team mom job is a part-time administrative role that gyms stopped paying for. Here's what it actually costs the person doing it.
headline: The "team mom" job is *unpaid labor*. We need to stop pretending it isn't.
sub: Somewhere in your gym there is one parent running a part-time administrative operation for free — work the program used to pay someone to do. The sport has normalized it. It should not have.

related.title: 20 things every new cheer mom wishes she'd known.
How to tell if a gym is actually good.

blocks.text: **Editorial note:** The workload described here is a composite illustrating patterns team parents report consistently across gyms. It is not drawn from a formal survey, and the hourly figures are illustrative. The argument does not depend on the precise numbers.

Every all-star team has one. She is usually the parent who has been around longest, who answers her phone, who is visibly competent. At the start of the season someone asks whether she would mind being the team parent, and because it sounds like a title rather than a job, she says yes.

What she has actually agreed to is a **part-time administrative position with no pay, no defined hours, no job description, and no ability to resign without disappointing thirty families and, implicitly, her own child.**
What the job actually contains
Ask any team parent to list what they do and the list is longer than they expect, because most of it is invisible until it stops happening:

items: **Hotel coordination** — negotiating or managing a room block for six to nine competition weekends, chasing families who haven't booked, handling the ones who cancel
**Payment collection** — gift funds, team meals, spirit items, banquet contributions; tracking who has paid and following up with people who haven't
**Communications** — running the team chat, translating gym announcements into plain language, answering the same question fifteen times because parents ask her instead of the front desk
**Competition-day logistics** — call times, warm-up schedules, meeting points, snacks, spare bows, the emergency safety pin supply
**Emotional buffering** — being the first person told when a family is upset about placement, competition time, or another family, and deciding what to escalate

blocks.text: That last one is the part nobody counts and the part that costs the most. **The team parent absorbs conflict that would otherwise reach the gym owner.** She is doing unpaid HR.
The arithmetic nobody does out loud

A realistic in-season workload is something like ten to fifteen hours a week, spiking well above that in the fortnight before a major competition. Add unreimbursed personal spending — printing, supplies, the gift nobody else remembered, the extra hotel night because she arrived early to check the block.
Priced at what a gym pays its own front-desk admin, a season of team-parent work is worth roughly *five figures*. Per team.

Multiply that across the thousands of all-star teams competing in the US and the scale of unpaid administrative labor the sport runs on becomes hard to look at directly — particularly because the people doing it are overwhelmingly women, and because their families are **already paying five figures a season for the privilege of being there.**
Why this happened
This is not a conspiracy. It is a slow structural drift, and it is worth understanding because it explains why the problem is stable.

All-star gyms operate on genuinely thin margins. Mat space is expensive, coaching staff is expensive, and insurance is expensive. When a program grows from four teams to twelve, the administrative load grows with it — but hiring a coordinator is a fixed cost against uncertain enrollment, while **asking a parent is free and requires no decision anyone has to defend.**

So the work migrates. First it's "can you collect for the coach gift." Then it's the hotel block. Then it's the group chat. Within a few seasons an entire role exists that nobody ever created, staffed by someone nobody ever hired.
The part that makes it hard to refuse

The reason this persists is that **saying no has a cost that lands on your kid, not on you.** A parent who declines worries — not always rationally, but not baselessly either — that she will be seen as uncommitted, that her athlete will be marked as coming from a family that doesn't contribute.
That is what makes it a trap rather than a choice. A volunteer role you cannot decline without social consequence is not really volunteering. It is an unpriced condition of participation.
What gyms should actually do
None of this requires a gym to be villainous, and the fixes are unglamorous:

items: **Pay a team coordinator and put it in tuition.** Spread across a full roster this is a small monthly line per family — far smaller than what families already absorb in unquantified fees, and it converts invisible labor into a visible, fair cost.
**Move logistics into software.** Team management platforms handle scheduling, payments, and rosters. Most of the team parent's job is being a human database that a $10/month tool replaces.
**Write the role down.** If a parent volunteer role must exist, it should have a scope, a time expectation, and an explicit end. Undefined roles expand indefinitely.
**Route conflict to staff.** Parents should not be the escalation layer for other parents' complaints about coaching decisions. That is the gym's job.

**Cap the team fund and publish the ledger.** If a program needs a large discretionary parent-collected fund, that is an accounting problem the gym should own, not a collection problem to hand a volunteer.

blocks.text: What to do if it's already you

If you are the team parent this season, the useful move is not martyrdom and it is not quitting mid-season. It is **making the work visible**, which is uncomfortable precisely because the role depends on it staying invisible.

items: Write down what you actually do and roughly how long it takes. Not to complain — to have a document when the conversation happens.
Ask the gym directly which of these tasks are its responsibility. Some of them will be, and nobody has ever asked.
Split the role. Hotels, payments, and communications are three jobs. One person doing all three is a staffing decision disguised as a favor.
Set an end date and tell people. "I'm doing this through May and then handing it off" is a complete sentence.

blocks.text: And if you decline the role next season: the athlete still gets her bows, the team still competes, the hotel block still gets booked. The world does not end. It just gets slightly harder for a system that was quietly relying on you.

CheerInsider articles are written with AI assistance. Cost figures and scenarios are illustrative, based on patterns reported across the cheer community — not original data collection or formal surveys.
